title: Plot Problems in “Once Upon a Time in the West”

commenti.body:
1. They trust Jill to make a deal. They know it's risky but Frank/Morton need to buy the property. If They kill her, buying the property becomes more difficult. Not a plot hole 

2. He was broken out by his men. Two of his thugs buy one way tickets after Cheyenne is at the station. This happens off screen. It's not a plot hole. 

3. They communicated via intermediaries. The key dialogue is "You're the one making appointments?" Meaning Harmonica met one of his gang who promised to setup a meeting. Frank setup an ambush instead. Not a plot hole.

thanks. im still thinking about your point 3. he is referring to Frank making appointments? Isn't frank then seeking Harmonica out.  and  then setting out to kill a man implies you know something about him. why not just meet first and hear him out? it might be a business proposal. but sending out 3 men makes it pretty clear no? that is an effort.

Harmonica is the one making appointments. Frank sends his goons because he can smell an ambush a mile away and has better things to do. Why should he care if someone wants to meet him? 

Frank has no idea who Harmonica is until he's about to die.

ok thanks. I take your point 2 and 3. but point 1 has issues

On the train Mton says to Frank, "the woman", Frank then replies "it's time I take care of her personally". It's the "personally" that is clearly a major threat to this woman. Yet no one seems to think of stopping him.  A serious plot hole.

I disagree with the specifics of these, but that's been covered. More relevant, though, is my general skepticism of elevating a hunt for "plot holes" in something as deliberately uncanny as a Leone western. This is a man who reveled in the implausible: Eastwood's three characters were practically gods in their ability with a gun, characters routinely can't see things in plain sight because they're offscreen, prison seems like a suggestion at best, that sort of thing. 

"Plot" in the conventional sense is tertiary to what makes Leone's films work, and so, even granting the existence of these *holes", their existence or lack thereof isn't central to my own appreciation of the film. What I take away from OUATITW has more to do with Leone's command of film form in all respects, his emotionality, and the way the film's many intertextual connections to other westerns build into a wonderful elegy for the genre.

I enjoyed the movie greatly and the overall ending.  But as a screenwriter these things do come up when I am watching. some are clarified throughout the movie that I totally missed.  others some are writing gaps and were not resolved satisfactorily for me.
I thought 'My Name is Nobody' was the elegy for the genre :)
That's the thing though, Leone's films aren't led from the screenplay. I understand that can be frustrating got a writer, but it's not the method Leone uses to create an effective and beautiful film.
tfw your genre has been elegized about ninety times.
This one literally has a tombstone for Sam Peckinpah in the graveyard
